title: Chapter 61: The Free Valleys, Part 5 of 5: Hild
html:
Hild did not take them straight to the loft.
She stood by the door after Granny Abbe had gone, big and quiet, with her red forearms folded, and looked at Corin's leg. She had been looking at it, he realized, on and off all evening, the way the others had looked at his hands.
"Sit," she said. "Again. On the bench. Put it up."
He did not argue. He was too tired to argue, and something in her voice made him think it would not have done any good. He sat on the end of the bench, and she pulled a stool across with her foot and lifted his bad leg onto it by the heel, as easily as if it were a child's.
"Breeches," she said.
The girl made a small sound. Corin looked at her. She had gone pink, and was looking very hard at the banner over the fire. Oren, who had been about to sit down again, changed his mind and went to stand by the hearth with his back to them all, warming his hands.
Corin undid his belt.
The wound was at the back of his left thigh, a hand's width above the knee. He could not see it without twisting round. He had only seen it once, in Silas's shaving glass, in the crypt: a small round hole, black at the edges, where the iron rod had gone in, and around it a wide ring of skin gone purple and yellow and green, like a bruise on an apple. Silas had cut it open, and drained it, and packed it with honey and lint, and left it open to heal from the inside. It had been healing. It had been healing well, Silas said, for a winter wound.
Hild bent over it with the lamp.
She looked for a long time. She did not touch it. Then she sniffed it, the way a cook sniffs meat, and straightened up.
"Who did this?"
"A doctor. In the city."
"Good doctor." She said it flatly, like a fact. "He knew to leave it open. They mostly don't, the city ones. They sew it shut and it goes bad under the stitches." She went to a shelf by the hearth and came back with a clay pot with a cloth tied over it, and a roll of clean linen. "Honey's good. This is better, for walking. Goose fat and yarrow. Keeps the cold out of it."
She untied the cloth. The smell was sharp and green and a little like old hay. She took the old dressing off, very quickly and very gently, so quickly that it was done before he had time to feel it, and laid a pad of linen thick with the green grease over the hole, and bound it round with a fresh strip.
Her hands were rough, and red, and very sure. They did not shake at all.
"You've done this before," said Corin.
"I've done it to cows." She tied the knot. "And to my brother."
She said it in exactly the same voice, flat and slow, as if there were no difference. But she did not get up when she had tied the knot. She stayed kneeling on the floor by the stool, with her red hands resting on her knees, and looked at his gray ones.
Corin waited.
"He went south," said Hild. "My brother. Rab. When he was nineteen. To the city, to work on the docks. Everybody said not to. He went anyway. Young men do." She was quiet for a moment. "He came back nine winters ago."
The girl had turned round from the banner.
"He came back over the drove road," said Hild, "in the snow, same as you. On his own. And his hands were like yours. Gray. Up to here." She touched her own arm, just above the elbow. "He couldn't feel them. He couldn't hold a cup." She looked at the black tips of Corin's fingers. "Black at the ends. Like that."
"What happened to him?" said Lyra, very quietly.
Hild did not look at her. She kept looking at Corin's hands.
"He said they'd made him burn," she said. "Down in the city. For the tax. Somebody's tax, not his. He said he'd burned for a man in a fine coat, over and over, and every time the gray went up, and every time they paid him a little and said once more. And then one morning he woke up and he couldn't remember our mother's face. And he got up off his straw and walked out of the city and walked north for six days, and came home." She stopped. "He said the gray was still going up. Even when he didn't burn. A little every day. He could feel it creeping. He said he'd be a Slate by spring."
Nobody said anything. The peat fire whispered.
"He stayed one night," said Hild. "In that loft. Then in the morning he kissed me, and he went up over the Lip, and he walked out onto the Glass." She looked up at Corin at last. Her eyes were pale blue, and quite dry. "He said nothing burns there. He said nothing can be taken there. He said if he was going to go gray, he'd go gray somewhere it would stop."
"Did it stop?" said Corin.
"I don't know." She got up off her knees, slowly, the way heavy people get up, one hand on the bench. "He never came back. Nobody comes back." She picked up the pot of green grease and tied the cloth over it again. "There's others. Not many. Every few winters. A man or a woman with gray hands, coming up the drove road in the snow, going north. Harvesters, Abbe says. City folk, burned out. They stop here a night, and they go up over the Lip in the morning, and they don't come back down." She held the pot out to him. "Take it. Change it every night."
Corin took the pot. His fingers could not feel it. He held it in both hands.
"I'm not going there to die," he said.
Hild looked at him for a long moment.
"No," she said. "Abbe says you're not." She turned away toward the ladder. "She says you walk like you're going home."
She went to the ladder at the back of the hall and lifted the lantern down from its hook, and stood waiting, with the light swinging in her big red hand, for them to come.
The Loft
The loft was over the byre, at the back of the hall, and you got to it by a ladder.
The ladder was the first hard thing. Corin stood at the bottom of it with his crutch and looked up at the square black hole in the ceiling, and Hild, the big quiet woman, looked at him and then at the ladder and then at him again, and without a word she took the crutch out of his hand and passed it up through the hole to Oren, who had gone first. Then she stood behind him on the bottom rung, solid as a wall, so that when his bad leg would not take his weight on the third rung and he swayed, she was there, and he did not fall.
He did not thank her. He tried to, at the top, but she had already gone back down and taken the ladder's lantern with her, and the door of the byre had shut.
The loft was long and low, and smelled of apples.
That was the first thing. Before anything else, before his eyes had got used to the dark, the smell came at him: sweet and cold and a little winey, the smell of apples kept all winter in straw. There were racks of them along one wall, he saw, when his eyes cleared. Long wooden racks with slatted shelves, and on the shelves, rows and rows of small wrinkled apples, red and yellow and russet, laid out so that none of them touched.
The rest of the loft was straw. Deep, loose, clean straw, heaped against the walls and spread over the floor, and on the straw, three piles of folded blankets, thick and gray and rough, the kind made from the wool of the valley sheep. Under the slope of the roof there was one small window, no bigger than a book, with a single pane of thick greenish glass in it. Frost had grown on the glass in feathers. The moon was behind it somewhere. It made the frost glow faintly white.
Below, through the floorboards, he could hear the cows. Two of them, by the sound. Breathing and shifting and once, deeply, sighing. Their warmth came up through the gaps in the boards, a thick, animal, comfortable warmth, with a smell of hay and dung that was not unpleasant at all.
Oren had already taken one pile of blankets to the far end of the loft, by the ladder hole, where he could see the way in. He lay down on his back without taking his boots off, with his sword beside him in the straw and his good hand on its hilt, and was asleep, as far as Corin could tell, before his head was all the way down.
The girl took the pile under the window.
Corin took the one in the middle.
He did not lie down at once. He sat in the straw with his back against a post and his bad leg stretched out in front of him, and took the green book out of his coat, and the stub of pencil, and opened the book on his knee.
There was no light, except the faint white of the frost on the window. It was enough. He did not need to see the letters. His hand knew how to make them, even crooked, even in the dark. That was one of the things that had not been burned.
FRIDAY. THE FREE VALLEYS. THISTLE FORD.
He stopped. He thought about the day.
MY FEET WENT LEFT AT THE TWO SISTERS. I DO NOT KNOW WHY.
A BOY ON A RIDGE LOOKED AT MY HANDS.
GRANNY ABBE. SHE HAS A PIPE SHE DOES NOT LIGHT. SHE SAYS THE DOLL IS FOR THE CHILDREN WHO GO OVER THE GLASS. SHE WILL NOT SAY WHO.
THEY WENT QUIET AT OREN'S NAME.
He stopped again. He held the pencil in his fist and thought about whether to write the next thing. Then he wrote it.
ASK THE ASHBORN.
He closed the book, and sat for a while in the dark with it on his knee, and then he reached inward.
Malakor.
The answer, when it came, was so thin that he was not sure at first that it was an answer at all. It was like a thread of cold air coming under a door.
...boy.
You're further away.
...yes. A long pause. Corin waited. When the voice came again it was a little clearer, as if the old man had gathered himself up to say it. North of here... I'll be quieter. Every step. When you're on the Glass itself... I don't know. I think I won't be here at all. Not gone. Only... quiet.
You've been on the Glass.
The pause this time was so long that Corin thought the thread had broken.
Don't be frightened of the quiet, boy, said Malakor at last. That's all I want to say. When I stop talking... it won't mean I've gone. It'll only mean you can't hear me. There's a difference. Another pause. There's always a difference.
Then nothing. Only the cows, and the apples, and the frost on the window.
Corin sat with that for a long time.
He did not know how long he had been sitting there when he heard the straw rustle under the window, and knew she was awake.
She was lying on her side with her back to him, wrapped in her gray blanket and the black coat over it. He could see the shape of her against the faint white of the window. She was not moving, but she was not asleep. He did not know how he knew. Something about the way she lay. Too still.
He thought about not saying anything. He thought about the rule, and about Oren on the road, and the candle in the dark room.
"Lyra," he said.
It was the first time he had said her name that day. He heard it go out into the loft and come back to him, small, off the slope of the roof.
The shape under the window did not move. But after a moment, very low, she said, "What?"
He had not thought about what came next. He said the first thing.
"What does your voice sound like? When you're happy?"
There was a long silence.
"What?" she said again. Differently.
"Your voice. I kept it. The only thing." He looked at the dark shape of her back. "I can hear it in my head. Saying my name. It's quick. And it's a bit cross. And it's a bit frightened underneath." He paused. "I've heard it all day, and it's always like that. Cross and frightened. I wondered what it sounds like when you're not."
The silence went on so long that he thought she was not going to answer at all, and he was beginning to wish he had not asked.
Then the straw rustled. She turned over, onto her back. In the faint white light he could see her face now, turned up toward the slope of the roof. Her eyes were open.
"You'll know it," she said.
"How?"
"You'll know it when you hear it." She was quiet for a moment. "You'll have to wait. I'm not—" She stopped. She drew a long breath and let it out. "I'm not very happy just now, Corin."
"No," he said. "I know."
"So you'll have to wait."
"All right."
She turned her head and looked at him, across the straw, in the dark.
"You're very annoying," she said. "Did you know that?"
"No. The book doesn't say."
She made a sound. It was very small, and it might have been anything. But he thought, lying down at last in his own blankets, with his bad leg aching and the cows breathing below him and the smell of apples all round, that it had not sounded cross at all.
Through the Floor
He could not sleep.
He had thought he would. He had been walking since dawn, and his leg ached from the hip to the heel, and the straw was deep and the blankets were warm and the loft was full of the slow, heavy breathing of the cows below. Everything in him wanted to sleep. He lay on his back with his hands folded on the green book on his chest and closed his eyes and waited for it to come.
It did not come.
After a while he opened his eyes again and looked at the roof.
The roof of the loft was made of turf laid over long poles, and between the poles he could see the underside of the turf, dark and rough, with pale roots hanging down out of it like hair. The moon must have moved, because the frost on the small window had gone from white to a faint silver-blue, and the light it gave was a little stronger. He could see the racks of apples along the wall. He could see the slope of the roof coming down to meet the floor. He could see, at the far end, by the ladder hole, the dark heap of Oren, and hear him snore: a long, rough, patient snore, like a saw going slowly through a log, and then a pause, and then the saw again.
And he could see the girl, under the window.
She was asleep now. He was sure of it this time. She had turned onto her side again, with her back to him, and her breathing had gone slow and deep and even, and once, just as he looked, she made a small sound in her sleep, a sound like a word with no letters in it, and pulled the blanket up over her ear.
He looked away. It did not seem right to look.
He lay and listened to the hum instead.
It was louder here than it had been on the road. Or he was more used to it, and so heard it more. He could not tell. It was there in the beams of the roof and the boards of the floor, a long, low, steady note, so deep that it was more like a feeling in the bones than a sound in the ears. It came from the north. Always the north. He could have lain there with his eyes shut and pointed straight at it.
And his feet wanted to go.
That was the strangest thing of all. That was what was keeping him awake. He lay on his back in the warm straw, tired to the bone, and his feet were cold, and they would not lie still. Every few breaths they moved. The left one first, then the right. Small movements, under the blanket. Not twitches. More like the movements of a dog asleep by a fire, when it dreams it is running. As if his feet, on their own, without him, were still walking. Still going up the left-hand road from the Two Sisters. Still going north, toward the hum, in the dark.
He lay still and let them.
That was when he heard the voices.
They came up through the floor. Not from the byre, where the cows were, but from the other side, beyond the wall where the loft backed onto the hall. There must have been a gap there, a crack between the boards and the stone, because the voices were quite clear. Low, but clear. Three of them. He knew two at once. Granny Abbe's slow hoarse lilt, going up at the ends of things. Hild, the big quiet woman, who did not say much, and said it slowly. And a man. He thought it was the man who had spoken at the river, the one Granny Abbe had stopped with her lifted hand.
"...in the gray," the man was saying. "That's all I'm saying, Abbe. They're coming. He said so himself."
"Aye. He said so himself." That was Granny Abbe. "He didn't have to."
"That's not—"
"He didn't have to, Ewan. He could have lied. He looked at me and thought about lying, and then he didn't." A pause. The click of a clay pipe against teeth. "I've known a lot of men who were running from them in the gray. Not one of them ever told me so at the ford."
"He's a harvester." The man's voice had gone lower, as if he did not like to say the word. "You saw his hands. You know what that is. That's Ash, that gray. That's dead men's memories, burned. He's one of theirs. He's Ministry."
"He was."
"Abbe—"
"He was, Ewan. Look at him. Look at the hands." Granny Abbe's voice was very quiet. "They've used him up. Whatever he was, they've used him to the shoulder, and then they've put his name on a list. I'd stake my last button on it." A pause. "And he's not one of theirs now. Them in the gray don't walk with a Vance."
Nobody said anything for a while.
"A Vance," said Hild at last, slowly, as if she were holding the word up to the light to look at it. "After all this time. A Vance, walking in off the drove road in the snow."
"He doesn't know," said Ewan. "Did you see his face? He doesn't know what his own name is."
"No," said Granny Abbe. "He doesn't. They've taken that too, I think. Or else nobody ever told him." The pipe clicked. "That's for Haverstock to tell him. Not me."
"And the girl?"
"The girl asked about the old dolls." A long pause. "The back-stitched ones."
Something changed in the silence that followed. Corin could not have said what. It was as if all three of them, below, had stopped breathing at the same moment.
"How would she know about those?" said Hild.
"She didn't. She'd seen one, that's all. A baby had it." Granny Abbe's voice went slower and lower, until Corin had to hold his own breath to catch it. "Give it to the one who comes after. That's what the lady said, when she left it. A lady in a blue cloak. Asking the way to the coast."
Nobody answered.
Below Corin, a cow shifted and sighed.
"I'll send Davin with them in the morning," said Granny Abbe at last, in her ordinary voice. "As far as the cross. Then the Lip. Then it's not ours anymore. It's the Ashborn's." A creak, as if she were getting up. "And if them in the gray come asking, we've seen nobody. Three days of snow. Nobody on the drove road. Not a soul."
"Aye," said Hild.
"Aye," said Ewan, after a while. Not happily. But he said it.
Footsteps. A door, somewhere, opening and letting in a breath of cold that Corin felt even through the wall, and then shutting again.
Then, just as he thought they had all gone, he heard Granny Abbe again. She must have stopped in the doorway. Her voice was very soft now, as if she were speaking to herself, or to the dark.
"That one," she said. "The gray one."
"What about him?" said Hild.
"Did you see him come down the road? Off the hill? In the snow?"
"I saw him."
"With that leg. With that crutch. On that road, that nobody's walked since the leaves came down." The pipe clicked once against her teeth. "He never put a foot wrong. Not once. Every bend. Every stone under the snow. He knew where it was before he got there."
A long, long pause.
"That one walks like he's been here before," said Granny Abbe.
Then the door shut, and there was only the cows, and the apples, and the long low hum in the beams.
Corin lay very still in the straw, in the dark, with his hands on the green book.
He had not been here before. He knew that. The page said he was born in a place called Oakhaven, and he did not remember it, and he had lived his whole remembered life in the city, in a room at the top of a tenement on Tallow Street, in a basement at the Ministry. He had never been north of the fens. He had never seen a drove road. He had never heard of the Two Sisters until today.
He was sure of all of that.
And under the blanket, in the cold, his feet would not lie still. They kept on moving, small and patient and certain, the left and then the right, the left and then the right. As if they were still walking. As if they had been walking this way, north, toward the hum, for a long, long time, and had only been waiting for the rest of him to catch them up.
